edits.english: Ravina said to Rav Pappa: Since you were not with us last night within the Shabbat limit of Bei Ḥarmakh, you did not hear that Rava raises a contradiction between two superior Mishnayot and teaches their resolution.

edits.hebrew: לא הוית גבן באורתא בתחומא: כלומר, חבל על שלא היית אמש בשבת אצלנו בתוך התחום שתוכל לבוא לבית המדרש ולשמוע.

edits.english: Ravina said to Rav Pappa: Since you were not with us last night within the Shabbat limit of Bei Ḥarmakh, Rav Pappa did not hear that Rava raises a contradiction between two superior Mishnayot and teaches their resolution.
Rava’s discourse was on Shabbat night, and Rav Pappa was not able to attend because he was outside the Shabbat limit (Rashi).

This Aramaic expression generally refers to the statements of the Sages that were cited in the study hall. In several places in the Talmud, a Sage is cited as having requested that another Sage tell him the superior statements (*mili me'alyata*) of a certain Sage, e.g., Rav, Rav Ḥisda, or Rav Yosef, that were mentioned in the study hall. In other places it is stated that a Sage requested of his colleagues that certain superior statements be attributed to him. A Sage who was absent from the study hall was liable to miss superior statements that were conveyed at the time.

A Shabbat limit is the border of a Jewish settlement or of the temporary residence of one or more Jews, determined at the onset of Shabbat. It is defined as two thousand cubits outside the residence. By rabbinic decree it is not permitted for a person to travel on Shabbat beyond this limit. On Shabbat Sages would leave their cities to deliver lectures and sermons in nearby villages. One’s ability to learn Torah on Shabbat was often dependent on his ability to travel to the locale to which the Sage would come without going beyond the Shabbat limit.

This city, also called Ḥarmakh, or according to other readings, Harman or Bei Harman, was located on the Shanvata River. Some propose that the source of the name is the Persian word harman, meaning granary.
Round wicker barrels were often used as beehives in antiquity. In modern Hebrew, the word kavveret means beehive.
